Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Senegal's rural police stations, primarily handled by Gendarmerie brigades, record case files, complaints, and incident reports using handwritten procès-verbaux (PVs) as mandated by the Criminal Procedure Code. PVs are drafted "sur le champ" (on the spot), signed on each page, with no mention of digital tools; originals sent physically to prosecutors. Francophone standard PVs are paper-based. Recent digital initiatives (e.g., cybercrime reporting portal 2026, e-Senegal police clearances, AFIS for Gendarmerie) focus on online services and central systems, not frontline rural recording. No evidence of digital case logging at rural stations; procedures imply paper-first, possible later entry at higher levels. Score 1: entirely paper-based at rural facilities.

revision_notes: Cited Criminal Procedure Code and Biometric Update source confirm PVs are paper-based and that recent digital initiatives (e-Senegal portal, cybercrime portal) are central/online services rather than frontline rural recording. A fresh search finds that since 2024 the Police and Gendarmerie have installed 50 'Points de Digitalisation des Amendes' (PDA) across 47 brigades nationwide (18 Gendarmerie, 29 Police), digitising the processing and payment of forfeitary traffic fines (Le Soleil, Jan 2025: 164,014 fines processed, 841.9m FCFA collected in 2024), with a February 2026 announcement extending this via body-worn cameras linked to digital fine-processing devices for both forces. This is a narrow function (traffic-fine processing only) rather than general case-file digitisation, but it constitutes genuine digital data capture at station/brigade level. Recalculated from 1 (Entirely paper) to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital); general case recording and PVs remain paper-based.
revised_comments: Rural police and gendarmerie stations in Senegal record case files, complaints and procès-verbaux (PVs) by hand, as required under the Criminal Procedure Code; PVs are drafted on the spot, signed on each page, and the originals are sent physically to prosecutors. Since 2024, however, the Police and Gendarmerie have rolled out 50 'Points de Digitalisation des Amendes' across 47 brigades nationwide, enabling digital processing and online payment of forfeitary traffic fines, and a further expansion involving body-worn cameras linked to digital fine-processing devices is under way from 2026. This gives rural stations a genuine, if narrow, digital capability limited to traffic-fine processing, while general case recording remains paper-based, placing the facility in the 'mostly paper - some digital' category.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Senegal, including health centers, posts, and huts, predominantly use paper-based registers for patient data recording at the point of service. Aggregate data from these facilities is compiled and entered into the national DHIS2 system at district or higher levels for reporting and analysis, but there is no evidence of routine electronic health records (EMR) or point-of-care digital entry in most rural facilities.Plan Stratégique Santé Digitale 2018-2023 Digital initiatives exist, such as pilots for electronic patient records in a few facilities (2 hospitals, 1 health center, 1 post as of 2025, covering 127k patients) and national programs like PDSS (Programme de Digitalisation du Système de Santé) supported by World Bank, targeting 20% EMR adoption in health centers by end-2025.WeAreTech Africa article;World Bank Digital Economy Project Key barriers include poor rural internet connectivity (only 51/1600 facilities connected baseline), unreliable power, lack of ICT-trained staff, high costs, and uneven health worker distribution.Plan Stratégique Santé Digitale 2018-2023 There is a significant gap between national ambitions (Digital Senegal 2025, PSSD for full interconnection) and rural reality, where paper remains default and digital is limited to pilots and aggregate reporting.

revision_notes: Original sources (Plan Stratégique Santé Digitale 2018-2023, World Bank PAENS/digital economy project document, WeAreTech 2025 article) confirm paper-based recording at point of care with aggregate DHIS2 reporting compiled at higher levels. Fresh searches confirm this remains the case: a BMC Public Health study (Jan 2025) on health districts including rural Kédougou/Saraya describes routine data collection via paper registers with monthly aggregate entry into DHIS2 by trained head nurses (many providers untrained in DHIS2 entry), and a DHIS2 malaria data-quality study confirms data collection 'starting with paper-based data collection at the health hut/DSDOM level' feeding into monthly aggregate DHIS2 entry. A WeAreTech article (April 2025) confirms the World Bank-funded PAENS electronic patient record pilot covers only two hospitals, one health centre and one health post nationally (127k patients registered), with expansion to six more regions planned for 2025 - still a small fraction of the primary healthcare network. Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed; no evidence supports a higher or lower score.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (health posts, centres and huts) in Senegal record patient data on paper registers at the point of care. Aggregate figures are compiled monthly, typically by trained head nurses, and entered into the national DHIS2 system at facility or district level for reporting, rather than captured digitally in real time; many providers, particularly midwives, have not been trained to enter data directly into DHIS2. A World Bank-funded pilot (PAENS) has introduced electronic patient records in a small number of facilities - two hospitals, one health centre and one health post as of April 2025, covering around 127,000 patients - with plans to extend to further regions during 2025, but this remains a small-scale exception against a backdrop of paper-based recording, poor rural connectivity and limited ICT-trained staff. The facility-level status is best described as mostly paper with some digital elements.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices (in communautés rurales, ~70% of population) and village auxiliaries predominantly use paper-based recording, with village chiefs issued notebooks for vital events like births. Forms (e.g., Form No. 1) are provided at point of service, and low rural birth registration rates (~29%) reflect access barriers.GFF Data Portal Some digital exists: >100 centers computerized (out of 587 total, some rural), local servers for data entry/backup.UNECA CRVS Snapshot Pilots include RAPIDPRO mobile app for birth capture in Kolda region (southern rural).UNECA CRVS Snapshot Recent efforts: digitizing 20M+ historical records, new digital platform/mobile app launched (2025), secondary centers in remote rural areas, but legislation to enable full digital processes pending; rural-urban disparities persist.BiometricUpdate Barriers: infrastructure/electricity in remote areas (rainy season isolation), training, legacy paper systems (1972 Family Code). National ambition for e-CRVS outpaces rural point-of-service reality, where paper remains default except isolated pilots/donor projects; no evidence majority rural facilities routinely digital at capture.

revision_notes: Original UNECA CRVS snapshot (2019 data) reporting >100 computerised civil registration centres out of 587, and paper notebooks used by village-level auxiliaries, is confirmed as still broadly applicable. Fresh searches show the picture persists into 2025-2026: at the ID4Africa 2025 AGM (June 2025), Senegal's National Civil Status Agency (ANEC) reported overall civil-event registration completeness of 91.2% but with a 'very big disparity' between rural and urban areas, and confirmed that draft legislation to formally enable digital civil-status procedures still awaits Council of Ministers/National Assembly approval, alongside a paper-register restoration programme (EUR 28m) for deteriorated archives. A May 2026 article confirms ANEC has digitised more than 19 million historical civil records by 2024 and has now partnered with the Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations to further roll out 'integrated management software' across civil registry centres nationwide, including remote/underserved areas, but frames this as an ongoing, not yet complete, modernisation. No source indicates rural point-of-capture recording has shifted to routinely digital; paper capture with a growing but partial digital layer (archival digitisation, pilot mobile tools such as RAPIDPRO in Kolda) remains the best-supported description. Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices and village-level auxiliaries in Senegal predominantly record vital events, principally births, on paper, with village chiefs using notebooks that feed into municipal civil-status centres. The National Civil Status Agency (ANEC) has digitised more than 19 million historical civil records and, from May 2026, is partnering with the Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations to expand digital management software to civil registry centres nationwide, including remote and underserved areas, while draft legislation to formally enable digital civil-status procedures still awaits parliamentary approval. Pilot initiatives, such as the RAPIDPRO mobile application used in the Kolda region, support digital capture of birth notifications in some rural localities. Overall civil-event registration completeness stands at around 91%, but with a marked rural-urban gap, and paper remains the default recording method at rural facilities alongside a growing but still partial digital layer.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Senegal has a functioning national Education Management Information System (EMIS) called SIMEN, which produces reliable annual statistical yearbooks on enrollment, attendance, completion, and teacher data. Data flows from rural primary schools through district (IEF) and regional (IA) levels to central SIMEN, with schools using performance-based contracts (PBCs) for reporting. No evidence of direct digital entry at rural school level; collection likely paper-based at facilities (e.g., logs, registers), aggregated digitally at higher levels, consistent with decentralized structure and rural infrastructure challenges (limited internet/electricity). Recent pilots: DHIS2-based EMIS aggregate data in two districts since 2024 (GPE KIX project), digital hubs in 70 rural primary schools (2023+), but not nationwide rollout. World Bank PAPSE project (2022) strengthens SIMEN capacity but focuses on central improvements. Score 2: predominantly paper with some digital pilots/aggregate reporting.

revision_notes: Original sources (DHIS2 Senegal implementation page, World Bank PAPSE project appraisal document) confirm SIMEN as the central EMIS with rural school data flowing through district/regional levels to the centre; the World Bank Project detail page (P169916) could not be re-fetched (dead link) so its content was verified via the PAPSE PAD instead. A 2024 Development Gateway research synthesis on education data-driven decision-making corroborates that 'matrices and questionnaires are sent from the centralised level to local authorities for completion, sometimes configured on tablets', but that 'limited connectivity at the school level means data is often input manually', consistent with predominantly paper-based capture at rural schools with some digital tools (tablets, SMS-based programmes) used in specific initiatives. The DHIS2-based EMIS pilot remains limited to two research districts since 2024 and produces aggregate, not facility-level point-of-care, data. No evidence found of a shift to majority-digital capture at rural primary school level. Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Senegal report enrolment, attendance and teacher data through the national Education Management Information System (SIMEN), with data typically recorded on paper at school level - registers, logs and completed questionnaires - before being aggregated at district (IEF) and regional (IA) level and entered into SIMEN, sometimes using tablets supplied for statistical campaigns. Limited and unstable internet connectivity in rural schools means that, even where digital tools such as tablets are supplied, data entry is frequently completed manually rather than in real time. A DHIS2-based EMIS pilot launched in 2024 in two districts under the GPE KIX research project produces aggregate rather than facility-level data. The facility-level status is best described as mostly paper with some digital elements, consistent with wider infrastructure constraints, including limited electricity access and computer availability in many primary schools.
